extracted.intended_audience: essayists and creative-nonfiction writers (writers and students learning the lyric essay form)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing lyric essays in creative nonfiction, describing core aims and four broad formal families (flash, segmented, braided, hermit-crab) and how they function. Useful for writers deciding form and technique for lyric nonfiction pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: visible / stand-out / unusual structure
rubrics_metrics.description: a piece of writing with a visible / stand-out / unusual structure that explores / forecasts / gestures to an idea in an unexpected way
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyric essays resist tidy taxonomies (the platypus metaphor). The structure should be noticeable and contribute to how the essay gestures to an idea rather than simply delivering exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core responsibility: intellectual movement / discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite formal looseness, the lyric essay still has the responsibilities of any essay: to try to figure something out, to play with ideas, to show a shift in thinking (however subtle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even experimental lyric work should enact thought or discovery; the form should serve an intellectual or perceptual shift rather than being merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach and tone: intuition, image, questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyric essays rely more on intuition than exposition, often use image more than narration, and tend to question more than answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor associative moves, sensory imagery, and open-ended inquiry. Aim for the whole to add up to more than the sum of parts; accept ambiguity and suggestion rather than tidy conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flash essays: length and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash essays are defined as being one thousand words or fewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should be short, sharp, and clarifying—illuminating a moment or realization the way a flash of light can. The impact or meaning should resonate beyond the word count. (Author-cited example: “Gyre” by Diane Seuss.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmented essays: visible divisions and white space
rubrics_metrics.description: Segmented essays are divided into segments that might be numbered or titled or simply separated with a space break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use white/blank space to allow the reader to pause, think, and digest each segment. Each section can introduce something new but should still belong cogently to the whole. Variants include fragmented, paratactic, collage, and mosaic approaches; segments may be deliberately broken or purposely glued together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Braided essays: recurring strands and pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Braided essays are segmented essays whose sections have a repeating pattern—the way each strand of a braid returns to take its place in the center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each return of a particular strand should be enriched by the other threads encountered between appearances. Braiding can function for containment, ornamentation, to hold something fast, or to create tension (e.g., stranding threads to counter forces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermit crab essays: borrowing an extraliterary form
rubrics_metrics.description: Hermit crab essays borrow another form of writing as their structure—recipes, labels, album notes, etc.—the way a hermit crab borrows another’s shell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The borrowed form can protect vulnerable content or act as a container for messy or prodigious material. These essays depend on the reader’s knowledge of the extraliterary form; the shell can draw the reader in and the content may 'lie in wait' and then burst beyond the confines of the adopted form. (Author cites Brenda Miller’s terminology.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridization: overlap and combinability of forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyric essays may combine forms—e.g., flash and braided, segmented and hermit crab—so a single essay can operate in multiple formal categories at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feel constrained to choose one category; think of forms as overlapping shapes (a square is also a rectangle) and allow formal hybridity to serve the essay’s aims.
